---
title: "Architecture"
---


This section is for anyone who wants to change the package, port it, or check
whether its numbers can be trusted. It assumes you have read the user guide.

## The shape of it

```
R/
  contract.R    the exchange contract and the bundled reference files
  read.R        reading and validating exports
  plots.R       the figures and the tables behind them
  agreement.R   the six reliability coefficients
  reliability.R intervals, per-code agreement, the kappa diagnostics
  unitizing.R   did the coders mark the same stretches at all
  gamma.R       agreement measured against the best alignment
  progress.R    saturation as a number, and coder drift
  discovery.R   how far from saturation, and how much further to go
  planning.R    how much material a study will need
  reporting.R   the COREQ and SRQR checklists
  stats.R       the inferential statistics
  spec.R        the plugin's own Vega-Lite charts, via vegawidget
inst/extdata/   contract + nine samples + expected.json
```

Dependencies run one way: the plotting functions call the table functions and
the statistics, never the reverse. Nothing in `read.R` knows about ggplot2.

## Every figure has a table

`qda_plot_frequencies()` is a thin layer over `qda_code_counts()`, and the
same holds for every other plot. Two reasons. First, users need the numbers
for supplements and reviewers. Second, the Python twin draws the same figures
from the same tables, and keeping the data preparation separate is what stops
the two from drifting apart in what they show.

## Reading is a checkpoint, not a convenience

`qda_read()` could have been a call to `utils::read.csv()`. Instead it checks
the format stamp, the version and the promised columns, and stops rather than
returning something plausible. The reasoning: a wrong number that stops the
script costs an hour, and a wrong number that does not costs a publication
correction.

The version check is deliberately asymmetric. Older versions are read; newer
ones refuse. A newer export may have renamed a column or changed a meaning,
and this package has no way to know which.

## Attributes rather than a class

A read export is a plain `data.frame` with `qda_format`, `qda_version` and
`qda_grain` attached as attributes. An S3 class was considered and rejected:
users want to hand these tables straight to dplyr, ggplot2 or `table()`, and a
class would only invite methods nobody needs. Attributes survive most
operations and cost nothing when they do not.

## Lists rather than S4 for results

`qda_chisq()`, `qda_mds()`, `qda_cluster()` and `qda_ca()` return named lists.
The point is that a caveat travels with the result: `expected_ok` sits next to
the test, `goodness` next to the coordinates, `cophenetic` next to the tree,
`inertia_share` next to the map. Returning only the interesting number would
make the caveat optional, which in practice means unread.

## Where MASS enters

`qda_ca()` is the only function that uses *MASS*, for `MASS::corresp()`. MASS
is GPL-licensed, which is compatible with the AGPL and therefore costs
nothing. The Python twin computes the same analysis from a singular value
decomposition, so if the dependency ever needs to go, the replacement is a
known quantity rather than a research project. See
[design decisions](design.qmd).

## Why gamma is its own file

`gamma.R` is the only place in the package with an exact combinatorial
search. Finding the best alignment is a set-partitioning problem, NP-hard for
three or more coders, and the implementation is a branch and bound with a
pruning rule and an admissible bound rather than a call to a solver -- which
would have meant a new dependency and, worse, a different answer from the
Python twin.

The search budget is deliberate. When it runs out the result is `NaN` with a
reason, never the best incumbent found so far. A gamma produced by a
heuristic is not gamma, and a number that is sometimes exact and sometimes
approximate is worse than no number.

## What is deliberately absent

* **No writing.** Nothing here modifies a Zotero library or an export. Coding
  happens in the plugin.
* **No caching.** Exports are small; a cache would only create a way for the
  data to go stale mid-session.
* **No tidyverse dependency.** ggplot2 is needed for the figures; beyond that
  the package uses base R, so it installs on a bare machine.
* **No non-ASCII in `R/`.** CRAN requires it, and it is checked.
